MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER 
Pursuant to Rule 213(a)(3) of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”) 
Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Community Organizations and Clean Energy Advocates 
respectfully submit this Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer to MISO’s Answer filed on 
September 23, 2026,2 which directly engages with Community Organizations and Clean Energy 
Advocates’ protest of MISO’s proposed Zero Generation Interconnection Service (“ZGIS”) and 
Zero Generation Interconnection Agreement (“ZGIA”) process.3 This Answer is timely because 
it has been filed within 15 days of MISO’s September 23 filing.4 
As described in the Answer below and attached testimony from Mr. Houtan Moaveni, 
Vice President at Grid Strategies LLC,5 MISO’s Answer does not redress the deficiencies of its 
proposal. Specifically, the proposed process does not ensure compliance with operational 
requirements, does not demonstrate that its cost allocation method is just and reasonable, and is 
not appropriately limited given the foregoing concerns. MISO’s Answer also only partially

MOTION FOR LEAVE 
Although the Commission’s Rule 213(a)(2) does not generally permit answers to 
answers,6 the Commission permits answers for good cause shown, including when an answer 
contributes to a more accurate, complete record or provides information helpful to the 
Commission’s decision-making process.7 This Answer will aid the Commission’s decision-
making process by providing additional perspective in support of the Community Organizations 
Protest from an electrical engineer with over a decade of transmission and interconnection policy 
leadership experience with utility and state organizations,8 as well as additional clarification of 
the Protest. Community Organizations and Clean Energy Advocates therefore ask that FERC 
accept this Answer. 
ANSWER 
Community Organizations and Clean Energy Advocates note three areas of concern that 
MISO’s Answer does not resolve: the failure of the proposed operational requirements to ensure 
that generators with ZGIA service (“ZG resources”) are genuinely zero injection such that they 
warrant expedited processing and do not risk reliability problems; the unjust and unreasonable

cost allocation methods that shift certain types of costs from ZG resources by socializing them 
more broadly; and the lack of system-wide limits on the ZGIA process, of which MISO fails to 
appropriately consider the broader implications. Finally, Community Organizations and Clean 
Energy Advocates appreciate MISO’s Answer regarding the eligibility for hybrid resources, but 
continue to encourage FERC to require that these clarifications be solidified in the tariff. 
A. MISO’s Answer Does Not Cure Concerns with ZGIA’s Operational Requirements.  
In their initial protest, Community Organizations and Clean Energy Advocates explained 
that MISO’s proposal fails to actually limit ZG resources to zero injections due to imprecise and 
permissive operational standards without adequate penalties and other incentives.9 MISO’s 
Answer attempts to defend this design, noting that its proposal “imposes specific operational 
requirements” to enforce ZGIS’s zero-injection limitation, including the required installation of 
communications and monitoring equipment by the ZG resource enabling it to monitor demand of 
the ZG Associated Load, as well as equipment to enable the Generating facility to reduce its 
injections within the Transient Tolerance Window.10 Community Organizations and Clean 
Energy Advocates do recognize that MISO’s proposal includes several measures facially 
designed to ensure that resources with ZGIAs comply with the operating requirements.11 But as 
Mr. Moaveni’s testimony further explains, these proposed measures leave several gaps.12 
By way of analogy, MISO’s requirements amount to requiring a car to have a 
speedometer, without imposing appropriate speed limits on the road, using radar detection for 
independent identification of speeding, or posting clear penalties to de-incentivize speeding.

Community Organizations and Clean Energy Advocates respond below to explain why the 
remaining uncertainty in implementation of the Transient Tolerance Window is akin to lacking 
appropriate speed limits. Further, inadequate verification of compliance testing is akin to not 
conducting independent speed checks, and reliance on solely a contractual remedy without 
intermediate remedies or financial penalties is akin to lacking clear and well-calibrated penalties 
for road violations other than cancelling a driver’s license. Finally, we explain that MISO’s 
emphasis on the distinction between interconnection and transmission service, though important 
to understand, does not dispel Community Organizations’ concerns. 
1. Neither Explanations in MISO’s Answer Nor Provisions in the Business Practice 
Manual are Adequate Substitutes for Tariff Rules Regarding Key Operational 
Terms of the Transient Tolerance Window. 
Community Organizations and Clean Energy Advocates’ Protest explained that MISO did 
not justify the tariff’s use of a twenty-second Transient Tolerance Window,13 and that MISO’s 
inclusion of supplemental terms in the Business Practice Manual violates the Rule of Reason.14 
MISO’s Answer does not remedy these concerns. First, MISO’s claim that the twenty-second 
maximum has a “reasonable engineering basis”15 relies on the fact that MISO uses a twenty-
second study period for other transient responses.16 But Community Organizations and Clean 
Energy Advocates’ concern is not about using twenty seconds as an interval for transient study 
generally, but rather, whether the operational consequences of exceeding the zero-injection 
limitation in this specific context cause reliability violations.17 As Mr. Moaveni puts simply, “the

Filing does not demonstrate that injections lasting up to twenty seconds are operationally 
acceptable.”18 That’s because while the “study horizon establishes the period analyzed, it does 
not by itself establish the maximum operationally acceptable duration of an unplanned export.”19 
As Mr. Moaveni states, “the permitted duration should be derived from what the system can 
tolerate at the location in question.”20 And as Community Organizations and Clean Energy 
Advocates explained in protest, the ZGIA process is unique in that it is entirely defined and 
justified by virtue of having zero injections.21 
Second, MISO defends the twenty seconds as a just a ceiling, with the potential to be 
lowered based on tests to be memorialized within the Business Practice Manual,22 but this is 
irrelevant since (a) as explained above, there are no demonstrated circumstances that the ceiling 
is  proven to be appropriate under, and (b) in circumstances in which the 20-second ceiling 
would not be appropriate, the applicability, enforceability, and functioning of the Business 
Practice Manual are all unclear and unreliable. It is well-established precedent that key terms 
must be included in the tariff.23 This precedent is important. A resource’s ability to limit its 
injections to its permitted tolerance window is a condition of ZGIS.24 MISO offers this service 
on the basis that resources can and will adhere to these conditions. Yet MISO proposes to leave 
the details of these conditions to the Business Practice Manual, a document that is developed 
through the stakeholder process and not filed with the Commission. As Mr. Moaveni explains,

MISO asserts that placing these critical rules in the manual ensures “consistent” treatment 
of ZG Interconnection Customers,26 but this assertion is unsupportable. Only the Tariff both 
applies equally and is enforceable. To be sure, some minor implementing terms can be 
appropriate for manual inclusion only. But in MISO’s proposal, the Tariff does not even 
explicitly dictate the baseline standard to which ZG resources managed through the Business 
Practice Manual would be held. As Mr. Moaveni explains, “the performance any such solution 
[pursued through the Business Practice Manual] must achieve is not stated in the Tariff.”27 
Without at least this much of a baseline standard in the Tariff, MISO’s filing provides insufficient 
evidence for the Commission to conclude that rates established by the proposal would be just and 
reasonable, and the filing is deficient.  
2. MISO’s Required Equipment Testing is Insufficient Verification to Confirm the 
Performance of Injection-Limiting Plans.  
Community Organizations and Clean Energy Advocates’ Protest also explained that the 
proposal does not sufficiently verify compliance with injection limits because MISO proposes to 
let ZG resources propose their own protection equipment systems,28 in tandem with a deferred 
evaluation by MISO of any “proposed control equipment and/or operating procedures.”29 As we 
explained, this open-ended and discretionary approach does not ensure ZGIS’ defining features

are met, nor provide adequate reliability safeguards. MISO now characterizes its choice to avoid 
any prescription of ZG resources’ specific technological approaches in favor of requiring only 
compliance with operational requirements as “performance-based,” which it argues will better 
adapt to the changing nature of technology.30 But this characterization imposes a tradeoff 
between baseline requirements and additional, more flexible performance standards that does not 
need to exist. MISO ultimately fails to demonstrate that stronger baseline requirements are 
unnecessary.  Moreover, the set of requirements proposed by MISO collectively fail to verify that 
a ZG resource’s injection-limiting scheme will actually perform according to plan.31 
MISO’s reliance on specific tariff and contractual provisions in its Answer only further 
highlights the inadequacies of its proposal.32 As Mr. Moaveni acknowledges, pre-operation 
testing and certain routine inspections and further testing as required by Articles 6.1, 6.2 and 
9.7.4.6 do indeed operate to ensure that the control equipment operates as it should under the 
Appendix A Interconnection Service level.33 But this is an insufficient scope. First, as Mr. 
Moaveni continues to explain, “none of [the proposal terms] expressly requires  a dynamic 
demonstration that, following a sudden reduction or loss of associated load, the facility can 
reduce its output to the load’s current withdrawal within the Transient Tolerance Window.”34 In 
other words, MISO’s proposed tariff fails to establish ZG-specific criteria or tests that confirm 
that a resource’s equipment will actually limit injections in operation.35 Second, while it’s 
generally beneficial that some testing is required, there is no requirement to report such results to

testing injection events or control failures to MISO.37 This impermissibly leaves verification of 
compliance with reliability requirements in the hands of ZG resources rather than the grid 
operator. 
In short, without “the Tariff [] stat[ing] the zero-injection obligation as a measurable 
performance criteria rather than as a general requirement to install suitable equipment … there is 
no assurance that the required equipment will perform as MISO’s studies assume.”38  
3. MISO’s Limited Remedies for Injection and Equipment Failures Fails to
Properly Incentivize Compliance with Performance Standards, Risking
Reliability Issues.
As Community Organizations and Clean Energy Advocates explained in Protest, MISO’s 
lack of remedies designed to incentivize ZG resources to ensure that their equipment will 
perform as required raises similar reliability issues as the lax verification measures.39 The 
contractual remedy that MISO has proposed functions only as a “last-resort backstop,” offering 
no consequence other than termination and nothing that operates on the timescale of an injection 
event.40 MISO relies on the pro forma generator interconnection agreement’s general default 
and termination framework instead of creating remedies tailored to deter or correct injections by 
ZG resources.41 While termination may be an appropriate response to persistent or repeated 
failures, termination alone is not an adequate option set as a remedy for noncompliance when

applied to protection-scheme misoperations.42 
As Mr. Moaveni explains in his testimony, MISO’s proposal only begins to cover 
violations of certain types of injections that could occur. Specifically, ZG resources may 
inadvertently inject power beyond their interconnection substations in three different situations: 
ordinary tracking errors, contingency-driven transient exports, and control or protection 
failures.43 Out of the three circumstances, control or protection failures involve the largest 
injections and will continue until the controls recover or corrective action is taken.44 Yetthe 
Filing does not establish a ZG-specific monitoring, testing, or remedial framework for control or 
protection failures.45 While the ZG Impact Assessment models a loss of load followed by a 
reduction within the Transient Tolerance Window, it does not model a sustained injection beyond 
it.46 Nor does the Filing contain automatic or graduated curtailment, suspension, or financial 
consequence that would give customers an adequate incentive to maintain and correct injection-
limiting controls.47 Article 9.7.4.7(c)’s obligation to cease injection when triggered by the trip of 
a transmission facility in the delivery path is also not enough to cure the deficiency in the Filing, 
as it is an operating requirement that responds to a system event, rather than a remedy for non-
compliance.48 In light of these serious risks, Community Organizations and Clean Energy

Advocates urge the Commission to direct MISO to include graduated penalties to incentivize 
better compliance with operational requirements. 
MISO answers that this docket is “not the appropriate vehicle” for considering penalty 
proposals, and states that it does not want to explore penalties here for certain types of generating 
facilities and service types.49 But neither FERC nor stakeholders like Community Organizations 
and Clean Energy Advocates can rely on such vague intentions about future filings. And as it 
stands, the proposed new ZGIS put forth for FERC’s approval lacks proper incentives and 
requirements for compliance that penalties could help remedy. As Mr. Moaveni explains, the 
penalties need not be limited to just penalizing exceedance of fixed interconnection service. 50 
Instead, Mr. Moaveni recommends that MISO should tie penalties to the zero-injection 
protection schemes on which the ZG interconnection service depends.51 In other words, MISO 
can, within this proposal, establish penalties for control equipment failure that need not pre-judge 
penalty scheme consistency with future products yet to come.52 We note that MISO’s avoidance 
of penalties in this context is newfound. MISO’s own previous ZGIA proposal to its stakeholders 
in June 2026 demonstrated that penalties would be appropriate for ZG resources and ZGIS. In a 
proposal to its Large Load Working Group in June 2026, MISO stated that it would “monitor 
each ZGIA for injections and will consider substantive charges for any injections.”53

MISO’s Answer also relies heavily on the distinction between interconnection and 
transmission service in order to minimize its proposal’s general permissiveness of violations of 
zero-injection requirements.54 For example, MISO states that the “ZGIS provides no general 
right to inject energy onto the Transmission System and does not convey Transmission 
Service.”55 MISO also quibbles that the twenty-second limit is not an authorization to inject for 
twenty seconds, but rather, the maximum interval “within which a project must satisfy the 
applicable study and operating requirements,” or potentially a shorter interval if determined by 
the Business Practice manual.56 But this is still accurately—and perhaps more tellingly—
described as a potential twenty-second period in which there are not clear consequences to the 
ZG resource for injecting, without adequate guarantee that there will not be reliability impacts as 
a result.  The issue is not that ZGIS or the Transient Tolerance Window provides a right to inject 
onto the Transmission System, but that ZGIS does not adequately penalize ZG resources when 
they do inject outside of or beyond the Transient Tolerance Window or adequately prevent them 
from doing so. The question is whether the Tariff attaches any operational consequence to 
injections, outside of or beyond the Transient Tolerance Window, onto the Transmission System 
beyond the substation.57 It does not. 
Finally, MISO invokes Order No. 845 in justifying its lack of penalties for unauthorized 
injections here.58 But as Mr. Moaveni explains, the potential exceedance of interconnection 
service level in other contexts that MISO discusses in its Answer is different than the ZG control

failures that are at issue here.59 A conventional generating facility has a fixed interconnection 
service level and went through an interconnection study where necessary Network Upgrades 
were identified.60 A conventional generator’s exceedance of that level would be a departure from 
a quantity that the system was studied to carry.61 In contrast, a ZG resource has no general right 
to export beyond the interconnecting substation and its permissible output is limited by the 
associated load’s current withdrawal, which can change abruptly.62 As Mr. Moaveni explains, 
“[t]he loss of the associated load does not itself change the [ZG] resource’s dispatch instruction 
on the seconds-scale of the Transient Tolerance Window, and the Filing caps the resource’s 
registered operating limits at the load’s peak Demand rather than its current withdrawal.”63  
Compliance depends on the injection-limiting scheme preventing a sustained export onto a 
system that was neither studied nor upgraded for it.64 Additionally, Order No. 845 “rested on the 
adequacy of existing interconnection agreement mechanisms for the exceedance it addressed,” 
but those mechanisms—monitoring, testing, and verification—are what the ZGIA now leaves 
incomplete for a control failure.65  
B. MISO’s Answer Fails to Disprove or Justify the ZGIA Process’s Creation of 
Potential Cost Shifts. 
Community Organizations and Clean Energy Advocates’ Protest explained two pathways 
that the ZGIS process allows for costs associated with ZG resources and large loads to be 
socialized more broadly: via the modeling overlaps between ZG and Definitive Planning Process

(“DPP”) resources, and via the risk that ZG resources relied on as transmission alternatives to 
support new load might not materialize, and thus the transmission need would have to be met 
through MISO’s Transmission Expansion Process (“MTEP”). MISO’s Answer continues to 
improperly assume that the definitional limits of ZGIS will prevent such cost issues—which Mr. 
Moaveni’s testimony explains in detail is not the case from an engineering perspective—and 
seems to misunderstand the concern related to crediting ZG resources as transmission 
alternatives. Despite these concerns, MISO also argues it should not yet be forced to provide 
enough transparency to detect potential cost shifts. The Commission should redirect MISO on 
these points. 
1. MISO’s Reliance on the Limited Nature of ZGIS Does Not Justify Socialization 
of Upgrades to Address Cumulative Grid Impacts. 
As Community Organizations and Clean Energy Advocates explained in Protest, the 
difference in assumptions built into the baseline of the study models for ZGIA resources and the 
DPP force upgrades arising from cumulative impacts between the two processes to be resolved 
through MTEP, where costs are broadly socialized.66 MISO does not contest the differences 
between the models, nor how conflicts would be resolved.67 Instead, MISO suggests that that the 
limits inherent to ZG service – namely peak load limits and the requirement to be at the same 
substation and voltage level – should generally serve to limit cumulative upgrade needs.68 But 
MISO’s assumption about ZG resources is not supported by evidence, and fails to otherwise 
justify socialization of costs that may nevertheless arise to cover upgrades to cover cumulative 
impacts on the  grid resulting from the addition of ZGIA resources.

MISO’s assertion that the defining limits of ZG resources will prevent grid strain from 
these resources does not withstand scrutiny. As Mr. Moaveni explains, “a generating facility 
affects the transmission system in ways that do not depend on whether it is exporting real 
power.”69 For example, “[a]n energized generator can contribute fault current to nearby buses 
even when it is not exporting real power.”70 This matters because the technology and grid 
functions that would address such issues – breaker interrupting capability and protection 
coordination margins at nearby substations – are “a finite and shared capacity on which pending 
DPP projects also rely.”71 As a result, the double allocation of access to such resources between 
ZGIA and DPP resources is not resolved by injection, substation or voltage requirements. And 
this is just one example of potential cumulative impacts. As Mr. Moaveni’s testimony further 
explains, merely “[p]reserving transfer capability therefore does not establish that ZG resources 
omitted from a DPP model, or DPP projects omitted from a ZGIA model, have no short-circuit, 
protection, voltage, or dynamic interaction with one another.”72 
The Commission should reject the filing as deficient because both MISO’s filing and 
MISO’s Answer fail to either refute such cumulative impacts or justify their resolution in MTEP, 
which socializes costs to load more broadly. 
2. MISO’s Defense of the 5-Year Contract Terms Misunderstands the Nature of 
Potential Transmission Cost Shifts. 
MISO’s filing allows for ZG generating facilities to be credited as non-transmission 
alternatives, which recognizes that the proximate nature of the facilities and intent for the load to

Protest, MISO’s filing contains no measures to backstop the cost and reliability issues this

MISO’s Answer appears to either misunderstand this concern76 or choose not to address it 
before the Commission. Yet as Mr. Moaveni testifies, MISO has previously acknowledged that 
“[i]f ZGIA agreements are not met and upgrades become necessary, those costs are still allocated 
to the load in the Local Pricing Zone,” and that “MISO is not proposing any changes to cost 
allocation of either generation or transmission investments in its ZGIA efforts. Cost allocation 
could be a component of the broader large load efforts taking place at the Large Load Working 
Group.”77 While MISO may not be changing cost allocation per se, as Mr. Moaveni explains, the 
associated large load in this situation would have already received the significant benefit of this 
proposal—namely, expedited connection to the grid.78 Moreover, the rapid emergence of 
transmission needs in such a scenario might cause further complications and more expensive

3. MISO Cannot Justify Exempting ZGIS from FERC’s Emphasis on 
Transparency to Prevent Large Load-Related Cost Shifts. 
Community Organizations and Clean Energy Advocates’ Protest explained that MISO’s 
proposal does not provide sufficient information to identify potentially deferred or shifted costs 
of transmission upgrades as a result of the large load associated with the ZG resource, and noted 
this conflicts with FERC’s Show Cause Orders on large loads.80 MISO answers that its ZGIS 
proposal need not address all of the issues raised in the Show Cause Orders.81 While we do not 
dispute this assertion in its entirety, it is misplaced here. The Commission should not allow 
MISO to add new processes to the tariff that suffer from the same flaws that the Commission has 
already found to be unjust and unreasonable—namely, lack of transparency surrounding cost 
causation.  
MISO further avers that the transparency measures requested by Community 
Organizations and Clean Energy Advocates are not required of requests in the Definitive 
Planning Phase, and that MISO does not propose to reduce any generally applicable transparency 
requirement.82 As Mr. Moaveni explains, comparisons to other processes are not relevant. “The

Q. How does the proposed contractual remedy, without additional measures, function to 
ensure compliance with the operating requirements? 
A. The proposed contractual remedy functions only as a last-resort backstop. It offers no 
consequence short of termination, and nothing that operates on the timescale of an injection event. 
The Filing relies on the pro forma generator interconnection agreement’s general default and 
termination framework rather than on a remedy designed to deter or correct injections by ZG 
resources. To see why that matters, it helps to distinguish the ways in which a ZG resource can 
inject power beyond its interconnecting substation. 
MISO refers generally to “inadvertent” or “unintended” injections, but those terms cover three 
different situations: ordinary tracking error, contingency-driven transient export, and control or 
protection failure. In an ordinary tracking error, generation briefly exceeds contemporaneous load 
by a small margin during normal operation. In a contingency-driven transient export, the associated 
load trips or drops sharply and the generating facility has not yet reduced its output. In a control 
or protection failure, the injection-limiting scheme does not arrest the export within the permitted 
window. These situations differ in likelihood and consequence, as well as in how they are detected 
and in the appropriate response. MISO’s proposed Transient Tolerance Window addresses 
contingency-driven transient export, and the proposed offer administration process addresses, at 
most, part of ordinary tracking error. No ZGIA-specific provision directly addresses the third 
situation, in which the facility continues exporting beyond the permitted tolerance because the 
mechanism intended to limit that export did not perform as expected. 
The situation in which exports continue beyond the tolerance window because a control 
mechanism fails is the situation in which a remedy matters most, for three reasons. First, it involves

11 
the largest injection, because absent a working scheme the facility’s full output can flow onto the 
Transmission System rather than the small margin of a tracking error. Second, it is not necessarily 
self-limiting; a transient export ends when the controls act, while a control failure can persist 
beyond the permitted window until the controls recover or corrective action is taken. Third, it is 
the situation the studies did not evaluate, since the ZG Impact Assessment models a loss of load 
followed by a reduction within the Transient Tolerance Window, not a sustained injection beyond 
it. 
Yet the Filing does not establish a ZG-specific monitoring, testing, or remedial framework for 
control failures. The ZGIA provisions contain no automatic or graduated curtailment, suspension, 
or financial consequence tied to an unauthorized injection that would give ZG customers a 
continuing incentive to maintain and correct their injection-limiting controls. The only contractual 
backstop is the agreement’s general breach-and-cure framework, which operates on a thirty- to 
ninety-day timescale suited to contractual defaults and, if the breach is not cured, leads to 
termination. Nor does Article 9.7.4.7(c) fill that gap. Its obligation to cease injection is triggered 
by the trip of a transmission facility in the delivery path; it is an operating requirement that 
responds to a system event, not a remedy for non-compliance. 
Termination, standing alone, is not a workable remedy for operating non-compliance. A ZG 
resource is by design dedicated to serving its associated load, and the Filing requires the associated 
arrangement to state an expected term of at least five years. Terminating the interconnection 
agreement would eliminate the generator’s interconnection rights and leave the associated load’s 
full demand dependent on network service. Without intermediate measures, termination provides 
no means of correcting an isolated or remediable control failure, and its consequences fall on the 
associated load as well as on the party whose equipment failed to perform. The injection-limiting

12 
scheme must act whenever the load’s withdrawal falls, not only when the load trips entirely, and 
termination removes the load’s dedicated supply for the remainder of the term, long after the event 
that triggered it. 
Termination can also create an immediate planning and operating challenge. Because the 
associated load remains firm network load, termination requires its full demand to be supplied 
from the Transmission System; where facilities have been deferred in reliance on the ZG resource 
and are not yet in service, MISO may need interim operating measures or accelerated construction, 
as discussed in Section IV. Termination may well be the appropriate response to persistent or 
repeated failure, but the Filing offers nothing before that point. Intermediate remedies should be 
available and applied proportionately to an isolated protection-scheme misoperation, repeated non-
compliance, and persistent failure. Those intermediate measures could include a ZGIA-specific 
cure period during which operating restrictions apply, mandatory load-rejection retesting after an 
injection event, temporary suspension pending correction, financial consequences for 
unauthorized injections, and escalation for repeated events, with termination reserved for the end 
of that sequence. 
The Article 17 cure period is not a substitute. It is not clear that a single injection event, once it 
has ended, is a Breach that can be cured in the Article 17 sense. If it is treated as cured once the 
scheme is restored, Article 17 itself imposes no injection-specific consequence for the completed 
event; if it is treated as a Breach that is not capable of being cured, Article 17 provides that the 
non-breaching Party “shall terminate” the agreement.16 Either way, Article 17 does not impose a

between cure and termination. 
Existing reliability standards do not fill this gap either. Protection-system misoperation reporting 
asks whether a protection scheme operated as it was designed to operate. It does not ask whether 
the scheme achieved the zero-injection obligation on which ZG Interconnection Service is 
premised. A protection system can perform exactly as engineered and still permit injections 
inconsistent with the terms of the interconnection service. 
Intermediate compliance measures of this kind are feasible. Indeed, MISO described a more 
complete compliance regime to stakeholders than the one in the Filing. When previewing the 
proposal to the Large Load Working Group in June 2026, MISO stated that “MISO will monitor 
each ZGIA for injections and will consider substantive charges for any injections; injecting more 
energy than the resource interconnection service limit can be cause for termination of the 
interconnection agreement.”17 Of the three elements in that sentence, only the last appears in the 
proposed Tariff. The ZGIA provisions impose no express obligation on MISO to monitor ZG 
resources for injections and establish no injection-specific charge. Narrowing a proposal after 
stakeholder review is not unusual. The point is that MISO itself identified monitoring, and a 
consequence short of termination, as appropriate components of this construct. The Tariff should 
establish that compliance framework rather than relying solely on the agreement’s general default 
provisions.

Commission directed PJM to establish penalty charges and other remedial action for unreserved

IV.  Modeling Assumptions and Cost Allocation 
Q. How could MISO’s proposal affect responsibility for transmission costs? 
A. Two features of MISO’s proposal bear on who bears transmission costs and when. The first is 
reliance on a ZG resource as a substitute for transmission. This does not necessarily change which 
customers pay for load-serving upgrades, but it changes when those upgrades are identified and 
leaves responsibility for them unresolved if the resource is lost. The second is the set of study 
assumptions used to approve ZG resources, which can cause interconnection-related issues to be 
addressed under planning cost-allocation rules rather than generator-interconnection cost-
allocation rules. I address each in turn. 
Q. What cost-responsibility issue arises when MISO relies on a ZG resource as a substitute 
for transmission? 
A. MISO attributes much of the value of a ZGIA to transmission planning. MISO’s witness states 
that only resources with an accepted interconnection agreement are eligible for inclusion in MISO 
Transmission Expansion Plan (“MTEP”) studies. MISO identifies this as a principal source of the 
ZGIA’s value. According to MISO’s witness, the ZGIA process will provide an agreement within 
ninety days, which permits the resource to be modeled as an input to the subsequent MTEP or 
Expedited Project Review load study for its associated load, creating “the potential for reduced

26 
total cost of transmission network upgrades needed to integrate the new load.”38 Attachment FF 
permits the resource to serve as a Non-Transmission Alternative that offsets upgrades that would 
otherwise be required to serve the load. Transmission upgrades that would otherwise be identified 
for the associated load may therefore be deferred or avoided in the planning case that includes the 
ZG resource. 
Now consider what happens if the ZG resource fails to materialize, retires early, or becomes 
permanently unavailable. The associated load is firm network load taking Network Integration 
Transmission Service on a gross basis, so a transmission need that had been reduced, deferred, or 
avoided in reliance on the ZG resource may re-emerge and be identified in a later MTEP cycle. 
Any resulting transmission solution would be classified and allocated under the applicable MTEP 
cost-allocation rules. The Filing does not assign that cost to the ZG interconnection customer, 
establishes no ZGIA-specific true-up, and does not trace later planning costs back to the 
arrangement on which the earlier planning assumption depended.

outcome directly when stakeholders raised the concern. Responding to what it characterized as

agreements are not met and upgrades become necessary, those costs are still allocated to the load 
in the Local Pricing Zone,” and that “MISO is not proposing any changes to cost allocation of 
either generation or transmission investments in its ZGIA efforts. Cost allocation could be a

The order of study also matters. Because ZG studies include only projects with executed 
agreements, a ZG request can be studied and approved against short-circuit and protection margin 
that earlier-submitted requests still pending in the queue would otherwise have been studied 
against. Requests that have not yet entered an active DPP cycle are then studied against a base case 
that already includes the ZG resource, and are assigned any upgrades that the combined effect 
requires. MISO’s Answer states that a ZG resource seeking Energy Resource Interconnection 
Service (ERIS) or Network Resource Interconnection Service (NRIS) must submit a new 
Interconnection Request and proceed through the DPP on the same footing as other requests,53 
which is correct as to injection rights; it does not address the short-circuit and protection margin 
the resource has already been permitted to use. In addition, the study provision states that MISO 
will perform short-circuit, stability, and steady-state analyses “if necessary based on the proposed

configuration.”54 Read most narrowly, that qualifier makes the steady-state thermal and voltage 
analysis discretionary; read more broadly, it qualifies all three. Either reading warrants further 
explanation given that the governing scenario includes rapid loss of a large associated load. 
The ERAS experience is relevant here as well, although the analogy is only partial. The ERAS and 
ZGIA pathways share several structural features: an expedited pathway operating parallel to the 
standard process, studied against models that exclude the pending queue, with reconciliation 
deferred to transmission planning and no mechanism to allocate later-identified costs back to the 
projects that triggered them. One difference is that ERAS projects receive injection rights and can 
therefore consume transmission headroom that standard-process customers were relying upon, 
while ZG resources receive no such rights and do not consume export headroom in the same way. 
The shared capacity a ZG resource can consume is instead short-circuit and protection capacity at 
nearby substations. The cumulative effects I am describing include short-circuit duty, protection 
coordination, voltage performance, and dynamic behavior. Ultimately, a zero-export restriction 
does not eliminate those effects, although their magnitude depends on technology, operating 
condition, controls, and system topology. However, the absence of a cap or sunset means the 
potential cumulative exposure is less bounded under ZGIA. ERAS was capped and time-limited, 
and ZGIA is neither.  
Q. Is there evidence of how excluding pending requests from expedited-study models 
operates in practice? 
A. Yes. The ERAS process has produced executed interconnection agreements, and one of them 
illustrates the mechanism directly. The public version of the Generator Interconnection Agreement

interconnecting at the Twinkle Substation 345 kV bus.55 
The agreement’s prior-queue accounting is defined to look only within the expedited pathway.

which are limited by their terms to “ERAS study projects,” and in this agreement both read 
“None.”56 Projects pending in the Definitive Planning Phase are not identified in the agreement, 
because the accounting was never defined to reach them. 
The service granted is also conditional on regionally planned transmission, consisting of 750 MW

expected in service until June 1, 2032.57 The customer’s own network upgrade is two new 345 kV

I rely on this agreement as evidence that when an expedited pathway defines its prior-queue 
accounting by reference to the pathway itself, that accounting can be empty even while projects 
remain pending in the broader generator interconnection queue. MISO describes the ZGIA process

Q. Does MISO’s proposal contain provisions that effectively address these cost-responsibility 
and cost-shift risks? 
A. No. The Filing contains several provisions that bear on the question, but none of them functions 
as a cost-responsibility mechanism for the load-serving upgrades I describe. 
First, MISO’s witness states that “[t]he contingent facilities listed in the ZGIA would only be those 
facilities in the model used for the ZGIA study.”61 This defines the customer’s exposure by 
reference to the model as it stood at execution. It therefore operates as a limitation on the 
customer’s responsibility rather than as a protection for others, and anything identified later 
through reconciliation falls outside it.

Second, Attachment FF conditions reliance on a ZG resource on an executed agreement that “is in 
place and must span at least the five year planning horizon.”62 The corresponding provision in the 
interconnection procedures requires only that the agreement “state an expected term of at least five 
years.”63 MISO acknowledges that the weaker formulation was deliberate, stating that, to 
accommodate commercial considerations, MISO “only requires that the agreement specify an 
intent to use the full output of the Generating Facility for at least five years rather than a firm 
commitment.”64 A stated expectation is not equivalent to a firm commitment, and the two 
provisions should be reconciled. Separately, the Filing does not explain why a five-year expected 
term is sufficient or what notice MISO would receive before the resource is lost, when the 
transmission facilities deferred in reliance on it may take several years to plan and build. 
Attachment FF itself explains that the five-year span is intended “to ensure the ability to provide 
adequate lead time for an alternative transmission solution should the contracts terminate,” which 
confirms that lead time, not the service life of the deferred facilities, is the relevant measure. 
Third, if the generating facility fails to achieve commercial operation by the date the transmission 
solution would otherwise need to be in service, or if the contract terminates, “the Transmission 
Provider may require the applicable Load Serving Entity to delay the in-service date of ZG 
Associated Load until such time as an alternative solution can be placed in service.”65 This is the 
Filing’s principal express response to pre-service non-performance, and it has four limitations. It 
is discretionary and is directed at the Load Serving Entity, which may not be a party to the ZGIA 
and does not control whether the generator is built. It operates only before the load is placed in

timing remedy rather than a cost remedy, because it can delay the load but does not address the 
cost or reliability consequences of the changed planning assumption. 
Fourth, the requirement that a ZG resource trigger no Network Upgrades beyond the 
interconnecting substation is a meaningful constraint on the interconnection study, but it does not 
address the cost-responsibility issue I have described. The upgrades at issue are those needed to 
serve the associated load, which are determined later, in a different process, under different cost 
allocation rules. MISO’s Answer relies on the same limitation and, for the reasons explained 
above, does not reach those load-serving upgrades. 
Fifth, MISO prohibits netting and requires the associated load to take firm Network Integration 
Transmission Service and pay for transmission, ancillary, and administrative services on a gross 
basis. That addresses the risk of co-located load avoiding its share of system costs. It does not, 
however, address responsibility for upgrades deferred in reliance on the ZG resource, which is a 
different question. 
To address these issues, I recommend that the Commission require MISO to study each 
arrangement both with and without the ZG resource so that the deferred-upgrade baseline is 
explicit; to identify and record every upgrade deferred in reliance on a ZG resource; to require 
financial security or a cost-responsibility agreement covering the documented incremental costs 
of interim measures or accelerated construction that would not have been incurred had the deferred 
need been addressed in the ordinary planning sequence; to conform the interconnection procedures 
to Attachment FF on the five-year term; and to establish defined restudy triggers and cost-
allocation rules for upgrades identified through model reconciliation.

Q. Does MISO’s proposal contain transparency provisions sufficient to allow later 
transmission needs and their cost consequences to be traced to the ZGIA process? 
A. No. The Filing’s one meaningful transparency provision is that executed ZGIAs will be filed 
with the Commission, because MISO has extended the tender, negotiation, and execution 
provisions of the interconnection procedures to cover them.66 Public availability of particular 
diagrams or equipment details may remain subject to confidential or Critical Energy/Electric 
Infrastructure Information (CEII) treatment. Filing the executed agreements is useful, but it does 
not provide the information needed to trace a later transmission need to the ZGIA process or to 
identify its cost-responsibility consequences. 
No Tariff provision requires MISO to publish the information that would be needed for that 
purpose. Nothing requires posting of ZG applications or their status. Nothing requires publication 
of the ZG Impact Assessment or ZG Facilities Study reports. Nothing requires disclosure of the 
size or identity of the associated load, of the Network Upgrades identified or deferred, of affected-
system study results, or of injection events. Mr. Keyser states that applications will be posted on 
MISO’s public website in a timely fashion,67 but that commitment appears in testimony rather than 
in the Tariff. 
The practical consequence is that the reconciliation and true-up mechanisms I recommend would 
be difficult for stakeholders to evaluate without additional published information. To determine 
whether an upgrade identified in a later MTEP cycle resulted from assumptions made in the ZGIA 
process, a party would need the ZG study results, the models and base-case vintage used, the

that is required to be public. Transparency is therefore integral to evaluating any reconciliation or

MISO’s Answer responds that these disclosures are not required of requests in the Definitive 
Planning Phase, and that MISO does not propose to reduce any generally applicable transparency 
requirement.68 MISO is not reducing existing transparency, but the question is whether existing 
procedures allow anyone to trace the linkage this service creates between a particular ZG resource, 
the load-serving transmission assumption made in reliance on it, and a later MTEP reconciliation. 
MISO’s statement that other interconnection requests do not receive the same disclosure does not 
establish that existing transparency is sufficient for that purpose. 
To provide sufficient information for affected parties to trace later transmission needs and their 
cost-allocation consequences, including any cost shifts, I recommend that the Commission require 
MISO to publish, subject to appropriate protection for genuinely confidential commercial and 
cyber-sensitive information: the ZG requests received in each quarterly study period, with 
megawatt quantity, technology, location, and status; the study reports and the base case used; the 
Network Upgrades identified and, separately, the upgrades deferred in reliance on each ZG 
resource; affected-system results; requests rejected for requiring upgrades beyond the 
interconnecting substation; and an annual report of injection events, control failures, and any 
enforcement actions. This recommendation is consistent with the transparency concerns the 
Commission identified in its order to show cause in Docket No. EL26-70-000.69

V.  Eligibility and Limitations on the ZGIA Process 
Q. Is the ZGIA process equally functional for all resource types? 
A. MISO states that the requirements are facially neutral, fuel-agnostic, and open to any resource 
regardless of technology.70 That is accurate as a matter of eligibility, but it does not follow that the 
ZGIA process is equally workable in practice for all resource types. A paired generation-and-
storage configuration is eligible to apply for a ZGIA. Because a Generating Facility may consist 
of “one or more generating unit(s) and/or storage device(s),” such a facility can proceed through a 
single Interconnection Request, occupy one quarterly study slot, and be subject to a single service 
cap under Section 3.11(v).71 MISO has also confirmed that a resource with ZG Interconnection 
Service is considered deliverable to its associated load for accreditation purposes, with the 
reference to “firm interconnection service” in the accreditation provisions referring to 
deliverability.72  
How storage charging would be treated in such a configuration, however, remains unresolved. 
MISO has stated in the stakeholder process that charging by a storage resource with a ZGIA “will 
follow the same process as other storage resources – storage charging is not considered during the 
interconnection queue process; instead, it is studied as an obligation to secure transmission service 
as a load.”73 That approach may be workable for a stand-alone storage resource, but it leaves four 
questions open in a co-located configuration, where the defining constraint is the relationship 
between generation output and a specific load: (1) whether energy used to charge the storage

component from the co-located generation constitutes a withdrawal requiring transmission service; 
(2) whether charging from the Transmission System increases the Demand of the ZG Associated 
Load and therefore the permissible level of ZG Interconnection Service under Section 3.11(v); (3) 
how a charging storage component is represented in the load-trip stability case required by Section 
3.2.5.2.1, given that a charging battery is itself a load that can be lost; and (4) how charging energy 
is metered and settled where the resource and the load must be metered separately. These questions 
are material to project design, study treatment, and commercial evaluation. Leaving them 
unresolved creates practical uncertainty for paired generation-and-storage projects and may 
complicate or discourage their use of the ZGIA pathway, even though those configurations are 
facially eligible. The questions should be answered in the Tariff rather than left to interpretation at 
the time an application is filed. 
MISO’s Answer now states that “[c]harging behavior that affects the studied configuration will be 
evaluated as part of the ZG Impact Assessment, consistent with MISO’s treatment of charging in 
the DPP study process.”74 That statement appears only in a pleading, and it differs from MISO’s 
stakeholder explanation that storage charging “is not considered during the interconnection queue 
process.” Moreover, MISO’s new response still does not address the service-cap, metering, and 
settlement questions above. The charging-study requirement, and the answers to those questions, 
should be stated in the Tariff. 
Q. In what ways is the magnitude and duration of the proposed ZGIA process limited? 
A. The Filing imposes several project-level eligibility constraints, while the program as a whole 
has relatively few cumulative limits. The project-level eligibility constraints include that the

generating facility’s Point of Interconnection must be at the same voltage level of the same 
substation as a Point of Withdrawal of the associated load; the amount of service may not exceed 
the total Demand of that load; the resource may serve no other load; the resource may not hold 
ERIS or NRIS concurrently; the resource may not require Network Upgrades beyond the 
interconnecting substation other than System Protection Facilities; and the applicant must submit 
at least 180 days before the earlier of commercial operation or the load’s need-by date, pay a 
$150,000 non-refundable study deposit, demonstrate 100 percent site control, and provide an 
executed agreement with the entity owning the associated load. 
The Filing also includes one express process-wide throughput limit, under which MISO will study 
no more than ten Interconnection Requests in each quarterly study period, with overflow rolling 
forward in submission order.75 That is a throughput constraint governing the rate at which requests 
are processed. It does not govern how many ZGIAs may ultimately exist, how many megawatts 
they may represent, where they may be located, or how long the program will run. 
Q. In what ways is the magnitude and duration of the proposed ZGIA process unlimited? 
A. The Filing contains no sunset date for the ZGIA process. It contains no aggregate cap on the 
number of ZGIAs that may be granted. It contains no fixed aggregate megawatt ceiling; each 
project’s service level is instead bounded by the associated load’s peak Demand, which may be 
several hundred megawatts or more. It contains no locational or electrical concentration limit, so 
ten requests in a single quarter may be located at electrically adjacent substations, with the

cumulative short-circuit and protection effects discussed in Section IV. It contains no requirement 
that a ZG resource ever transition into the standard interconnection process. 
The proposal also contains no fixed limit on the duration of an individual agreement. ZG 
Interconnection Service is offered as a permanent product. I further note an inconsistency on this 
point. The transmittal letter describes the service as available on a permanent basis “subject to 15 
year automatically renewing term provisions,” but the filed form of agreement leaves the initial 
term blank and provides for automatic renewal in successive one-year periods.76 Whichever MISO 
intends, the term should be stated in the filed agreement. 
Because the quarterly cap governs processing rate rather than cumulative volume, and because 
there is no aggregate megawatt ceiling, the total quantity of generation interconnected on ZG terms 
is limited only by how long the process operates. At ten requests per quarter, that is up to forty 
requests studied each year and two hundred over a five-year planning horizon, with no limit on 
how many may ultimately receive agreements. MISO states that it does not expect to receive more 
than ten such requests per quarter as the process matures, and describes the cap as a safeguard in 
case the product proves more popular than expected.77 That statement indicates that actual uptake 
remains uncertain. 
The ERAS process provides a useful comparison. The Commission accepted ERAS as a parallel, 
expedited interconnection pathway only with a cap of sixty-eight projects and a sunset of August 
31, 2027, whichever came first.78 ZGIA proposes a permanent parallel pathway with neither.

Q. What are the likely adverse consequences of not limiting the ZGIA process beyond the 
ten-project quarterly cap? 
A. There are two principal consequences. First, the Filing does not examine how a growing share 
of generation dedicated to specific loads affects resource adequacy for the rest of the system. A 
ZG resource may not serve any load other than its associated load, and its capacity credits must be 
used in a Fixed Resource Adequacy Plan or Reliability-Based Demand Curve opt-out rather than 
offered into the Planning Resource Auction.79 Whether that matters depends on whether the 
pathway displaces generation that would otherwise have interconnected through the standard 
process with the ability to serve other load, or supports generation that would not otherwise have 
been built. The Filing does not address that question or explain how MISO’s loss-of-load modeling 
and planning reserve methodology account for ZG resources.80 
Second, a permanent construct reduces the opportunity to evaluate actual operating experience 
before the pathway becomes an enduring feature of the Tariff. This is a largely new construct, and 
MISO acknowledges having accommodated zero-injection arrangements only in limited 
circumstances in the past.81 A pilot with an initial term and an aggregate cap would permit the 
Commission and stakeholders to observe how many resources actually use the pathway, whether 
the injection limits hold in operation, and whether upgrades are later identified in transmission 
planning that were not anticipated in the interconnection studies, before the service becomes a 
permanent feature of the Tariff. Nothing about a sunset would deny the pathway to projects with 
near-term needs; it would simply require MISO to return to the Commission with an operating

record before the arrangement becomes permanent. The uncertainty about actual uptake that MISO 
itself acknowledges reinforces the case for an initial aggregate cap or sunset, accompanied by 
operational reporting. 
MISO’s Answer does not change this assessment. MISO argues that an aggregate cap or defined 
term is unnecessary because each ZGIA is limited by its same-substation configuration, its service 
cap, the prohibition on Network Upgrades beyond the interconnecting substation, and the ten-
request quarterly limit.82 Each of those is a limit on an individual project or on the rate of 
processing. None constrains how long the parallel pathway operates, how many agreements 
accumulate under it, or the aggregate generating capacity interconnected outside the Definitive 
Planning Phase. MISO’s Answer also confirms that MISO adopted the quarterly limit “to avoid 
disruption to the DPP and ensure that sufficient resources are available to process ZGIA 
requests.”83 That is a processing constraint, not a limit on the scale of the program.
